title: The Hospitality Owner's Guide to Receipt Paper Sizes
description: 2¼" vs. 3⅛" thermal rolls, kitchen vs. customer receipts — match the right size to every printer in your restaurant.
body:
Ordering the wrong receipt paper is one of the most common — and most avoidable — supply mistakes in hospitality. The printer jams mid-rush, the roll doesn't fit the spindle, or you end up with a box of paper you can't use. This guide walks you through the sizes that actually matter so every printer in your restaurant, café, or bar keeps running through the dinner rush.

The Two Sizes That Matter Most

Thermal receipt paper for hospitality comes in two widths that cover the vast majority of printers on the market. Once you know which one each of your machines uses, reordering becomes a five-second task.

  • 2¼" (57mm) — the narrow roll. Common in handheld order printers, smaller guest-check printers, and many bar or countertop setups. If you need a compact slip rather than a full-page receipt, this is usually it.
  • 3⅛" (80mm) — the standard-width roll. The workhorse for full-size POS receipt printers at the register, in the kitchen, and behind the bar. More room per line for itemized detail, tax, and tip lines.

If you're not sure which you have, don't guess. The width is printed right on the old roll's cardboard core or on a label inside the printer's paper tray.

Match the Paper to the Printer, Not the Brand

Thermal printers are largely forgiving about brand, but unforgiving about two physical specs: width and core size. Width is the obvious one. Core size — the diameter of the cardboard tube in the center — is the one that quietly trips people up.

  • Core size: Most 3⅛" rolls use a ½" core, but some models (especially older or specialized kitchen printers) need a 1" core. A 1" core on a ½" spindle will wobble and feed unevenly.
  • Roll diameter: Bigger diameter means more paper per roll and fewer change-outs, but it has to fit inside the printer's paper compartment. Check the maximum roll diameter before you upgrade to a longer roll.

The quickest way to get this right: pull the empty core, read the specs printed on it, and match them exactly on your next order.

Kitchen vs. Customer Receipts: Don't Mix Them Up

Many operators use one paper size at the register and a different one in the kitchen — that's normal and worth being deliberate about.

  • Kitchen printers often use 3⅛" rolls because tickets need room for modifiers, course timing, and table numbers. High-heat environments can also favor certain thermal coatings that resist darkening or curling near grills and steam.
  • Customer receipts at the counter may be either size depending on your POS hardware. A 2¼" roll keeps the slip compact for fast-casual and grab-and-go, while 3⅛" gives you space for a loyalty message, QR code, or survey link.

Keeping a clearly labeled reorder list — one line per printer, with width, core size, and diameter — prevents the "wrong box on the truck" problem entirely.

Buying Tips That Save a Headache

Beyond size, a few habits keep your paper supply reliable and cost-effective.

  • Store rolls flat and dry. Heat and humidity can make thermal paper darken prematurely or curl, which causes jams.
  • Buy the right length for your volume. Longer rolls mean fewer mid-shift change-outs but cost more per roll. Match roll length to how busy each station gets.
  • Check coating quality for kitchens. If tickets near heat are fading or sticking together, ask about higher-heat thermal stock rather than assuming all paper is the same.

Conclusion: Know Your Specs, Then Reorder

Receipt paper isn't a one-size-fits-all item, but it's simple once you nail down two numbers per printer: width and core size. Match those, size the roll length to your volume, and keep kitchen and counter paper separate. The payoff is fewer jams, fewer change-outs, and no dead stock sitting on a shelf.

Your next step: pull one empty core from each printer, write down the specs, and keep that list near wherever you place supply orders.
